Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

one pronoun

people in general

also you (in general), people, they say, one says

classical

Cic. Sen. 21: crēdō, nisi eam exerceās
Cic. Amic. 22: quīcum omnia audeās sīc loquī ut tēcum

persōna secunda (tū)

construction: the verb in the second person singular, mostly subjunctive

one, you (anyone at all)

The everyday way: “you”, meaning anyone, in the second person singular, in the subjunctive in a subordinate clause or a potential statement (nisi eam exerceās, if one doesn’t exercise it; crēderēs, you would have thought). Latin has no word for the pronoun “one”.

Other words

  • verbum impersōnāle passīvum — one (says, goes, lives): “it is said”

    construction: the passive, impersonally or with the thing as subject · classical · Plin. Ep. 7.5.1: ut vērissimē dīcitur; Cic. Sen. 49: ut dīcitur

    ut dīcitur, as one says; ītur, one goes, people go; vīvitur, one lives.

  • quis (sī quis, nē quis) — one, anyone (after sī, nisi, nē, num)

    pronoun, indefinite · also used · classical · Petr. 34.1: sī quis nostrum iterum vellet mulsum sūmere

    See someone.

  • persōna prīma plūrālis — one, we (people in general)

    construction: the verb in the first person plural · also used · classical · Catull. 22.21: sed nōn vidēmus manticae quod in tergō est

    Where the speaker includes himself: nōn vidēmus, we (one) don’t see.

Examples

  • at memoria minuitur. crēdō, nisi eam exerceās

    But memory fades. — I suppose it does, if you don’t exercise it.Cic. Sen. 21

  • quid dulcius quam habēre quīcum omnia audeās sīc loquī ut tēcum?

    What is sweeter than to have someone to whom you dare say everything as you would to yourself?Cic. Amic. 22

  • Māne quod tū occēperis negōtium agere, id tōtum prōcēdit diem.

    Business you begin in the morning goes well the whole day.Plaut. Pers. 114–115

  • ad diaetam tuam ipsī mē, ut vērissimē dīcitur, pedēs dūcunt

    My feet take me to your room by themselves, as is very truly said.Plin. Ep. 7.5.1

  • suus cuique attribūtus est error; sed nōn vidēmus manticae quod in tergō est

    Everyone has been given his own fault; but we don’t see the part of the bag that is on our back.Catull. 22.20–21

  • sī quis nostrum iterum vellet mulsum sūmere

    if any of us wanted another glass of honeyed winePetr. 34.1

See also oneself, someone, you.
